articles.title: The Man Who Stepped Out of Line
articles.dek: In a death camp in 1941, a priest gave his life for a stranger. The apostle John shows how that same love can be lived out on an ordinary day.
articles.quote: Laying down your life for someone usually happens in small installments, and God counts every one.
articles.illustration: Maximilian Kolbe takes a prisoner's place
articles.body:
The roll call at Auschwitz on that summer day in 1941 had already gone on for hours. A prisoner had escaped from Block 14, and the camp's rule for an escape was simple and cruel: ten men from the same block would be locked in an underground cell and left to starve. The prisoners stood in the heat while the deputy commandant, Karl Fritzsch, walked the rows and pointed at faces. One of the men he chose, a Polish army sergeant named Franciszek Gajowniczek, broke down where he stood. "My wife," he cried. "My children."

Then a thin prisoner in round wire glasses stepped out of line, something that in that place could get a man shot where he stood. He was prisoner 16670, a Franciscan friar named Maximilian Kolbe. He took off his cap and spoke quietly to the officer. He was a Catholic priest, he said, and he wanted to take this man's place, because the man had a wife and children. Fritzsch, perhaps too startled to argue, agreed.

Kolbe went down into the starvation bunker with the other nine. Prisoners who worked in that building later said that the usual sounds from those cells were screaming and cursing, but from this cell they heard prayers and hymns. Kolbe stayed with the men as they died, and after two weeks, when he was one of the last still alive, he was killed by lethal injection on August 14, 1941. Franciszek Gajowniczek survived the war and lived to the age of 93. He spent much of the rest of his life telling anyone who would listen about the man who died so that he could go home, and in 1982 he sat in St. Peter's Square as Kolbe was declared a saint.

Filipinos understand this story from the inside. We know the cry of a parent who thinks of the children waiting at home, because we have heard it in every tearful goodbye at the airport departure gate. We also know the kind of person who steps forward and quietly says, "Ako na," let me carry this one. Kolbe's act moves us because it is the clearest picture of love most of us can imagine. The apostle John wrote about exactly this kind of love, and what he did with it is good news for ordinary people like us.

John was an old man when he wrote this letter, most likely from Ephesus near the end of the first century, to churches he tenderly calls "dear children" (1 John 3:18). Those churches had been wounded by a split. A group had walked out (1 John 2:19), claiming a superior spiritual knowledge and teaching that Jesus had not truly come in the flesh (1 John 4:2–3). That is why John urges his readers to "test the spirits to see whether they are from God" (1 John 4:1). Their teaching was polished, yet it left people cold, and John offers his readers a simple test that anyone can apply: real faith in Jesus shows up as real love for people.

He begins with the oldest message the church knew: "We should love one another" (1 John 3:11). Then he reaches all the way back to the first two brothers on earth. "Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother" (1 John 3:12). Cain had watched God accept his younger brother Abel's offering, and jealousy grew in him until he lured Abel into a field and killed him. When God asked where his brother was, Cain answered with a question that has echoed through history: "Am I my brother's keeper?" (Genesis 4:9). John gives the answer across all those centuries, and the answer is yes. Cain took his brother's life to protect his own pride. Then John turns from the first murder to the cross.

"This is how we know what love is: Jesus Christ laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters." (1 John 3:16)

If John had stopped there, most of us would quietly file this verse under "heroes only." We admire a Kolbe, and we assume we will never stand in a yard like that one. John, however, does not stop. His very next sentence comes down from the heights into a kitchen or a sari-sari store: "If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in that person?" (1 John 3:17).

The Greek words make the connection beautiful. In verse 16, the word for the "life" Jesus laid down is psychē, a person's very life and self. In verse 17, "material possessions" translates ton bion tou kosmou, literally "the life of the world." The word bios means livelihood, the means by which a life is kept going: rice on the table and wages in the envelope. John sets two words for life side by side. One way to read this is that if Christ's love would move you to lay down your psychē for a brother, it will certainly move you to lay down some of your bios for him today. Laying down your life for someone usually happens in small installments, and God counts every one.

John's phrase "has no pity" carries a picture too. Literally, it says the person "shuts his splanchna," the inner parts where the ancients felt compassion, the way we might say someone closes the door of the heart. Filipinos have a word for that inner place: loob. When we speak of kagandahang-loob, the goodness of one's inner self, we mean goodness that cannot stay inside and must come out in what we do. That is what John is asking for, and he says it plainly: "let us not love with words or speech but with actions and in truth" (1 John 3:18). Kind words matter, but John wants love that can be seen and held.

Kolbe's own life shows how this works. The moment at roll call did not come from nowhere. Before the war, at his friary at Niepokalanów near Warsaw, Kolbe and his brothers had sheltered thousands of refugees, many of them Jewish, feeding them from the friary's own supplies. Years of sharing his bios had shaped a heart that, when the moment came, was ready to give his psychē. Small acts of open-handed love are how God trains a person for great ones, and most of the time the small acts are the whole assignment.

So the call of this passage is within your reach. Perhaps it is the younger cousin whose tuition is short this semester, or the neighbor whose maintenance medicine ran out a week before payday. It may be a coworker who needs an hour of your time more than any amount of money. Before this day ends, you could name one person whose need you have already seen, and keep your loob open long enough to do one concrete thing for them, however small it looks.

Some readers will feel a weight rising as they read this, because they remember the times they saw a need and looked away. John writes for you, too. He says that when we love in action, we "set our hearts at rest in his presence: If our hearts condemn us, we know that God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything" (1 John 3:19–20). The God who knows everything knows your failures, and he also knows every small kindness you have forgotten, and his verdict over you is mercy. Love begins with what was done "for us" (1 John 3:16) at the cross, and we love from that gift.

Franciszek Gajowniczek lived more than fifty years as a man whom someone had died for, and it shaped how he spent every one of them. That is your identity too. Jesus stepped out of line and took your place, and you get to go home. Live today as someone who has been loved like that, and let a little of that love spill out of your hands toward the next person in need.

articles.title: Then I Got Up
articles.dek: Daniel saw thrones of fire and the fall of empires, and the vision left him flat on his back. What he did next may be the most practical verse in the whole book.
articles.quote: The God who holds the end of history is also the God who hands you the next small task, and doing it well is one way of trusting him.
articles.body:
In a coastal barangay in the Visayas, the morning after a strong typhoon has a sound of its own. Before the power returns and before the news vans arrive, you can hear brooms scraping mud off concrete, a hammer knocking a loose sheet of yero back into place, and somewhere down the street the wooden shutters of the neighborhood bakery being pulled open. The panadero may have lost part of his roof in the night. He may have sat awake until dawn with his family, counting the gusts and praying the walls would hold. Yet by five o'clock there is a short line outside his window, and the smell of warm pandesal drifts over the wet street like a quiet announcement that life is still going on.

People abroad like to praise Filipino resilience, and many of us have grown a little tired of the compliment, because it can become an excuse for others to let us keep suffering. The baker's choice deserves a warmer name. After a night he did not choose, he got up and did the ordinary good thing his neighbors needed. He cannot fix the weather or restore the grid, but he can make bread, and so he makes it.

That small scene is a surprisingly good doorway into two of the strangest chapters in the Bible. Daniel 7 and 8 are full of beasts, horns, thrones and angels, and they belong to an old man. These visions came to Daniel in the first and third years of King Belshazzar (Daniel 7:1; 8:1), around 550 BC. By then Daniel had lived in Babylon for roughly half a century. He had been carried off as a teenager in 605 BC, trained in a pagan court, and had outlived Nebuchadnezzar himself. Now, probably in his late sixties or seventies, he was shown things that would have shaken anyone.

In the first vision, Daniel watched the four winds of heaven churn up the great sea, and four beasts climbed out of the water one after another (Daniel 7:2–3). First came a lion with the wings of an eagle, and after it a bear with ribs between its teeth. A leopard with four wings and four heads followed. The fourth creature had no animal name at all. It had iron teeth, it crushed and devoured whatever it found, and on its head a small horn sprouted with human eyes and a mouth that spoke boastfully (7:4–8). Then the scene shifted from the churning sea to a courtroom. Thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat, his clothing white as snow and his throne flaming with fire (7:9). The books were opened, and the beast was destroyed.

Then Daniel saw a figure who changed the meaning of everything before it. "There before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into his presence. He was given authority, glory and sovereign power" (7:13–14). Chapter 7 is written in Aramaic, the everyday language of the empire, and the phrase there is bar enash, which simply means a human being. After a parade of devouring animals, God hands the everlasting kingdom to someone with a human face. Centuries later, standing on trial before the high priest, Jesus would take that very picture and claim it as his own (Mark 14:62).

Two years later the second vision came, and the language of the book switches back to Hebrew. Daniel found himself beside the Ulai Canal in Susa, watching a powerful ram charge in every direction until a goat with a single prominent horn came flying from the west, so fast its feet did not touch the ground, and shattered it (8:3–7). For the first time in Scripture, an angel is named. Gabriel came to explain the vision, and Daniel collapsed with his face to the ground. Gabriel touched him and raised him to his feet (8:18). The ram, he said, was the kings of Media and Persia, and the goat was the king of Greece (8:20–21). History bears this out in striking detail: Alexander the Great swept east two centuries later, died at thirty-two in 323 BC, and his empire was split among his generals, just as the great horn was broken and four others rose in its place (8:8, 22).

After all of that, the chapter ends with a verse most readers hurry past.

"I, Daniel, was worn out. I lay exhausted for several days. Then I got up and went about the king's business. I was appalled by the vision; it was beyond understanding." (Daniel 8:27)

The Hebrew word for the king's business is melakhah, an ordinary word for work, craft and daily labor. It is the same word Genesis uses when it says God finished the work he had been doing in creation (Genesis 2:2). One way to read Daniel's return to the office, then, is as a small echo of the Creator's own pattern. God works, God rests, and God works again, and his servant does the same. Daniel had just watched empires rise and crumble on the screen of heaven. He knew Babylon itself was living on borrowed time, and within about fifteen years it would fall to the Persians in a single night. Still, after a few days in bed, he went back to the king's paperwork, the king's correspondence, and the king's people.

This suggests something tender about what faithfulness looks like after we have seen too much. Daniel did not pretend the vision had left him untouched. He admitted that he was worn out and appalled, and he confessed plainly that he did not understand it. Earlier he had said much the same: "I was deeply troubled by my thoughts, and my face turned pale, but I kept the matter to myself" (7:28). His honesty gives us permission to be shaken. He also shows us that being shaken is a season and need not become a home. The kingdom he had seen belonged to the one with a human face, and the best way to live in a world of beasts is to keep showing up with a human face yourself, serving the people right in front of you.

Many Filipinos know Daniel's exhaustion from the inside. The headlines this month alone are heavy enough: political quarrels that never seem to end, a strong El Niño gathering strength, forecasters watching the Pacific for one more storm before the year closes. Add to that the private news that never reaches the papers, such as a diagnosis, a remittance that did not come, or a child who has stopped calling home. It is possible to read and scroll until you are lying on your bed for several days, so to speak, unable to make sense of any of it. Daniel would understand. He would also gently remind you that the throne in heaven is still occupied, and that the next small task is still yours to do.

The God who holds the end of history is also the God who hands you the next small task, and doing it well is one way of trusting him. For some of us, that task today is answering a parent's message with patience. For others it is finishing the report, sweeping the sari-sari store, cooking for the household, or being kind to the tricycle driver who is having a hard week too. None of these will appear in a vision of thrones and clouds, but every one of them is a small sign of the kingdom that will never be destroyed (7:14).

If you are tired today, rest without guilt, the way Daniel lay down for several days and the way Gabriel lifted him gently to his feet. Then, when you are ready, get up and open your shutters like the panadero after the storm. You may still find the world beyond understanding, and that is all right. Choose one ordinary piece of work this morning, do it carefully and kindly, and offer it quietly to the Ancient of Days, whose kingdom is already on its way.

articles.title: A Song for the Night Shift
articles.dek: The last pilgrim song in the Psalms was sung to the few who kept the temple lamps burning while the city slept. Three short verses, and they were written for anyone whose faithfulness happens in the dark.
articles.quote: God sees the hours no one else sees, and he keeps a blessing with your name on it waiting there.
articles.body:
In the winter of 1854, the Barrack Hospital at Scutari, across the Bosphorus from Constantinople, was crowded with British soldiers brought in sick and wounded from the Crimean War. The corridors seemed to run on forever, and the men lay on thin mattresses in rows so close together that a visitor could barely pass between them. Florence Nightingale had arrived that November with a small band of thirty-eight nurses, and she worked through the daylight hours like everyone else. What made her name, however, was what she did after the doctors had gone to bed.

A correspondent for The Times of London described it in a dispatch that families back home read aloud at their tables: "When all the medical officers have retired for the night, and silence and darkness have settled down upon those miles of prostrate sick, she may be observed alone, with a little lamp in her hand, making her solitary rounds." She stopped at bedsides, wrote letters for men who could not hold a pen, and sat with the dying so that they would not die alone. A few years later the American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow imagined the scene in verse, writing of how "the speechless sufferer turns to kiss / Her shadow, as it falls / Upon the darkening walls." The name stuck, and to this day she is remembered as the Lady with the Lamp.

Much of the faithfulness that holds our world together happens in hours like those. Somewhere tonight a nurse will check an IV line at three in the morning while a mother in another city rocks a feverish child in a dark and silent house. Nobody applauds at that hour, and most of the people who benefit will never know it happened. The Bible, as it turns out, contains a song written for exactly these people.

Psalm 134 is the last of fifteen psalms that each carry the heading "A song of ascents" (Psalms 120 to 134). Most scholars understand them as pilgrim songs, sung by Israelite families as they climbed the roads up to Jerusalem for the great yearly festivals. Read in order, they trace a journey. Psalm 120 begins far from home, among people who hate peace, and the songs climb steadily toward the holy city until Psalm 133 celebrates the joy of God's people gathered together, "like precious oil poured on the head" (Psalm 133:2). Psalm 134 comes at the very end, and it sounds like the last song of the last night, when the festival is over and the crowds are about to scatter back to their villages.

Picture it with me. The courts of the temple have emptied. The pilgrims are bedding down in tents and courtyards, ready to leave at first light. Up on the temple mount a few lamps still burn, and beside them stand the Levites on night duty, the men whose job was to keep watch and keep worship going while everyone else slept. First Chronicles describes them as musicians who "stayed in the rooms of the temple and were exempt from other duties because they were responsible for the work day and night" (1 Chronicles 9:33). Before going home, the people turn toward those quiet figures in the lamplight and call out to them.

"Praise the LORD, all you servants of the LORD who minister by night in the house of the LORD. Lift up your hands in the sanctuary and praise the LORD. May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who is the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 134:1–3)

Many readers hear two voices in this little psalm, and the conversation between them is lovely. In the first two verses the departing pilgrims speak to the night servants, honoring their hidden work and urging them to keep lifting their hands in worship through the dark hours. In the third verse the servants answer back with a blessing for the people. One way to read it, then, is as a farewell exchanged between the many who are leaving and the few who are staying behind to keep the lamps lit.

The Hebrew makes the exchange even more tender. The word the NIV translates "praise" in verses 1 and 2 is barak, the same verb translated "bless" in verse 3. Many scholars link it to berek, the word for knee, because blessing in the ancient world was often given or received while kneeling. So the psalm traces a circle: the night servants bless the Lord, and the Lord blesses his people. Blessing rises from the dark temple and comes back down on the sleeping camp. Then there is a small detail most English readers miss. The "you" in "May the LORD bless you" is singular in Hebrew, the same intimate form used in the great priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24, "The LORD bless you and keep you." Thousands of pilgrims are leaving Jerusalem, and the blessing falls on each of them one by one, as if spoken to a single face.

The final phrase matters too. The Lord who blesses from Zion is "the Maker of heaven and earth," which means he is the maker of the night as well. On the very first page of Scripture, "God called the light 'day,' and the darkness he called 'night'" (Genesis 1:5). The dark hours belong to him as fully as the bright ones. A few psalms earlier the same pilgrims had sung that "he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4). The servants keeping watch in the temple were keeping company with a God who was already awake.

Filipinos understand night work better than most. Our nurses have become, in a sense, the world's night shift, keeping watch over strangers in hospitals from London to Riyadh to New York, just as Nightingale once did at Scutari. At home, thousands of call center agents cross EDSA at midnight to begin their workday, answering voices from the other side of the planet. Security guards doze-proof themselves with kape at the gates of sleeping subdivisions, and parents sit up with sick children long after the house has gone quiet. If you are one of them, Psalm 134 suggests that the place where you keep watch can become a sanctuary. Your hands may be busy with charts or a headset or a baby's bottle, yet the God who made the night is near you there, and your faithfulness in those hours rises to him as worship.

The psalm also has a word for those of us who sleep through the night. The pilgrims did not slip away without thanking the people who served while they rested. It would be a small and beautiful act of obedience this week to learn the name of the guard at your gate, or to tell a nurse on the night ward that you are grateful, or to pray for a family member whose shift starts when yours ends. Blessing given to the unseen ones has a way of returning, just as it did in that ancient courtyard.

Florence Nightingale's lamp was a simple folding lantern, nothing grand, and the light it threw reached only a few beds at a time. Yet to a frightened soldier at two in the morning, that small circle of light meant he had not been forgotten. Psalm 134 makes the same promise on a larger scale. God sees the hours no one else sees, and he keeps a blessing with your name on it waiting there. Tonight, whether you are clocking in or turning out the light, you can speak the last line of the pilgrims' song over yourself or over someone you love who is working in the dark: "May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who is the Maker of heaven and earth."

articles.title: The King Who Got His Feet Wet
articles.dek: A medieval king sat in the surf to silence his flatterers. Proverbs explains why a smooth word can do more harm than a hard one, and how the gospel gives us a better way to speak.
articles.quote: Love tells you the truth about the rising water, and then wades in to stand beside you.
articles.body:
On a beach in southern England, nearly a thousand years ago, a king ordered his servants to carry his throne down to the edge of the water. He was Canute, a Danish-born ruler who by the 1020s governed England, Denmark, and Norway, which made him one of the most powerful men in northern Europe. His courtiers had grown fond of telling him that his word could do anything. So, according to the twelfth-century chronicler Henry of Huntingdon, Canute sat down facing the incoming tide and spoke to it as a master speaks to a servant, commanding it not to rise onto his land or wet the robes of its lord. The sea kept coming, as seas do, and washed over his feet and soaked his legs.

Then Canute stood, stepped back, and turned to the men around him. "Let all men know how empty and worthless is the power of kings," he said, "for there is none worthy of the name but He whom heaven, earth, and sea obey by eternal laws." Henry adds that the king later hung his golden crown on a crucifix and never wore it again. Historians cannot prove the scene happened exactly as told, and popular memory has turned it upside down, picturing a vain monarch who thought he could command the ocean. The Canute of the chronicle is a far humbler man. He let the water soak him on purpose, so that his flatterers would have to watch the tide answer them.

Every one of us keeps some kind of court. It may be a group chat, an office, a church ministry, or a family table, and in each one there are voices that tell us what we want to hear. Long before Canute sat in the surf, the book of Proverbs had already studied those voices closely and given them an honest name.

Proverbs 26 reads like a gallery of portraits. The chapter opens with the fool (verses 1 to 12), moves to the sluggard who will not get out of bed (verses 13 to 16), then to the meddler and the gossip (verses 17 to 22). It closes with the most dangerous figure of all, the person whose words are lovely and whose heart is not. These sayings belong to the collection of Solomon's proverbs that, according to Proverbs 25:1, "were compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah," a royal court that would have known a great deal about flattery. Verse 23 sets the scene with an image from the potter's shop: "Like a coating of silver dross on earthenware are fervent lips with an evil heart." A cheap clay pot could be glazed to shine like silver, and only when you lifted it, or dropped it, would you learn what it was made of.

The next verses describe that shining pot in motion. "Enemies disguise themselves with their lips, but in their hearts they harbor deceit. Though their speech is charming, do not believe them, for seven abominations fill their hearts" (Proverbs 26:24–25). In Hebrew, seven is the number of fullness, so the picture is of a heart crowded to the brim with schemes. Yet the deceiver never gets the last word. "Their malice may be concealed by deception, but their wickedness will be exposed in the assembly" (26:26). Then comes a picture any village farmer would understand: "Whoever digs a pit will fall into it; if someone rolls a stone, it will roll back on them" (26:27). Finally the chapter ends with this sentence.

"A lying tongue hates those it hurts, and a flattering mouth works ruin." (Proverbs 26:28, NIV)

Most of us file flattery under kindness that has gone a little too far. We think of it as harmless sweetness, the extra compliment that keeps everyone happy. Proverbs places it in a much darker drawer. The same verse that speaks of flattery speaks of hatred, and the parallel suggests that the two belong together. One way to read this is that flattery is a quiet form of hostility, because it treats a person as a tool to be managed. The flatterer wants something from you, whether your favor, your vote, your money, or simply your silence, and he is willing to let you walk toward harm to get it.

The Hebrew words sharpen the picture. The word translated "flattering" comes from chalaq, which means smooth or slippery. It is the same word Jacob uses in Genesis 27:11 when he worries, "my brother Esau is a hairy man while I have smooth skin," just before he deceives his blind father. Psalm 55:21 uses it of a betrayer whose "talk is smooth as butter, yet war is in his heart." The phrase "works ruin" translates midcheh, from a root that means to push down or thrust over. Taken together, the image is of a smooth surface that makes a person slip, followed by a hand that gives them a little shove.

That is why Canute's courtiers were more dangerous than any army on his borders. A king who believes he can command the sea will one day make a decision that drowns real people. Proverbs gives the alternative in the very next chapter: "Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses" (27:6). It even promises that honesty wins in the long run, since "whoever rebukes a person will in the end gain favor rather than one who has a flattering tongue" (28:23).

Here the gospel shines brightest, because God is the one voice in the universe that never flatters us. He tells us the truth about our condition with complete clarity, "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Yet his honesty always comes joined to his love, for "God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). Canute hung his crown on a crucifix as a confession that his power was small. At the cross itself, the true King of heaven, earth, and sea wore a crown of thorns (Matthew 27:29) and gave himself up for people who could not save themselves. The gospel tells us the hard truth about the rising water, and then the King himself wades in to carry us out.

Filipinos understand this passage from the inside. We have words for the flatterer, the bolero who feeds us bola, and for the person who is plastik, smiling to our face and speaking differently behind our back. We also carry a deep and beautiful love for pakikisama, the art of keeping relationships smooth. That gift is good, and yet it can tempt us to choose the pleasant word over the true one, especially with those we love most. Paul's ministry offers a better pattern. He reminded one church, "You know we never used flattery" (1 Thessalonians 2:5), and urged another to grow by "speaking the truth in love" (Ephesians 4:15).

Practically, this works in two directions. Because the gospel has already told you the worst about yourself and still called you beloved, you can afford to welcome honest friends, so consider asking one person you trust to tell you something you may not want to hear, and thank them when they do. And when you speak to others today, let your praise be true and specific, and let your correction be gentle and patient, so that your words build people up instead of pushing them toward a fall. Love tells you the truth about the rising water, and then wades in to stand beside you. That is what Christ has done for you, and by his grace, it is what your words can do for someone else before this day is over.
